scenes.headline: How a transformer skips most of its own FFN
scenes.sub: Model casting: compute the gate, then skip the dead units.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Rosalind! A transformer's feed-forward network does most of the work per token. Here is how to skip most of it.

scenes.text: Train the feed-forward network so about ninety percent of its hidden units output exact zero, then skip the two big matrices for the dead ones.
scenes.say: The idea: train the feed-forward network so most hidden units output exact zero, then skip the two heavy matrices for the dead ones.

scenes.title: Compute the gate, skip the dead units

steps.say: First, run the gate matrix for every hidden unit. This matrix always runs. It is what tells us where the zeros are.
The R plus S activation sends the negative half straight to zero, so most hidden units go dark.
Only the live units touch the up matrix. Every dark unit skips a whole row of it.
They skip the down matrix too. We ran the gate, then skipped two matrices out of three.

scenes.title: Why the gate caps the win

left.title: Standard gate
left.say: With a standard gate, the full gate matrix runs every token. You can skip the other two, so the speedup tops out at three times.

right.title: LoPA gate
right.say: Make the gate low-rank and nearly free, then spend the saved budget on the big matrices. Now the speedup climbs past three times.

scenes.title: FFN speedup at ninety percent sparsity
scenes.say: Measured on a five point eight billion model, the GPU runs the feed-forward network two times faster with a standard gate, and over three times faster with the low-rank gate.

scenes.text: The always-on gate was the whole ceiling. Make it cheap, and ninety percent sparsity turns into real speed.

recap: Compute the gate, skip the dead units
The gate caps the win at three times
LoPA makes the gate cheap and breaks it
scenes.say: To recap: compute the gate, then skip the dead units. The gate caps the win at three times, and the cheap gate breaks past it.
